name: Claude Code and Codex CLI, compared command for command
description: Where Claude Code 2.1.220 and OpenAI Codex CLI 0.146.0 ship a command for the same job, what only one of them has, and how they differ on sandboxing, permissions, hooks and configuration.

source.method: The command halves are set operations over the two inventories published on this site, which were themselves read out of the installed builds. Descriptions are each build's own string, unedited. Which two commands count as the same job is a hand-made judgement — that is the one part of this file that was not measured — and the unpaired lists are then the computed complement, so every command appears exactly once. The capability rows come from `claude --help`, `codex --help` and the on-disk config layout of both tools; each carries how it was established.

fields.id: Stable anchor on the canonical page; append as #id to deep-link
fields.job: The shared job, named by hand — this is the editorial part
fields.claudeCode: The Claude Code commands and launch flags that do it, with their own descriptions and a link to the full entry
fields.note: Where the two differ in kind rather than in name
fields.onlyClaudeCode: Every Claude Code command no pairing claimed
fields.onlyCodex: Every Codex command no pairing claimed
fields.capabilities: Differences a command list cannot show, each with its evidence
fields.verdict: Opinion, derived from the rows above and marked as such

capabilities.claudeCode: ~/.claude/settings.json — JSON, with a /config UI and a bundled skill that rewrites it for you.
capabilities.codex: ~/.codex/config.toml — TOML, layered. Any key is overridable per-run with -c foo.bar=value, and --profile <name> stacks $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml on top.
capabilities.establishedBy: Both files on this machine, plus codex --help.

capabilities.claudeCode: CLAUDE.md, written by /init, auto-discovered up the tree.
capabilities.establishedBy: Each tool's own /init description, and both files present in the two config homes.

capabilities.claudeCode: One axis. --permission-mode takes acceptEdits, auto, bypassPermissions, manual, dontAsk or plan, with allow/deny rules per tool underneath.
capabilities.codex: Two orthogonal axes. --ask-for-approval takes untrusted, on-request or never; --sandbox independently takes read-only, workspace-write or danger-full-access.
capabilities.establishedBy: The [possible values] block each CLI prints for those flags in --help.

capabilities.claudeCode: /sandbox toggles sandboxing for the Bash tool, on supported platforms only. It applies to what Claude Code runs.
capabilities.codex: The same sandbox is also a command you can point at anything: codex sandbox -- <cmd> runs it under seatbelt, and --log-denials prints the macOS denials it collected.
capabilities.establishedBy: codex sandbox --help; the /sandbox description in the build.

capabilities.claudeCode: --dangerously-skip-permissions, plus --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions to make it available without turning it on.
capabilities.codex: --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, and separately --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust for running hooks whose source has not been vetted.

capabilities.claudeCode: Configured under hooks in settings.json. The binary carries eleven event names: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, Notification, PreCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop, SubagentStart, SubagentStop.
capabilities.codex: A separate ~/.codex/hooks.json, with per-hook trust recorded back into config.toml under hooks.state — Codex will not run a hook it has not been trusted to run.
capabilities.establishedBy: Event names read out of the Claude Code binary; the Codex side read off the two config files. See the caveat below the table.

capabilities.claudeCode: 35 compiled into the binary — the whole prompt corpus is on its own page here — plus whatever is in ~/.claude/skills. 23 of the bundled ones are typeable as slash commands.
capabilities.codex: /skills, loading from ~/.codex/skills and from plugins. Whether Codex also bundles prompts of its own is not established here — no equivalent extractor was written for it, and a Rust binary does not give them up the way a Bun-compiled JavaScript bundle does. Read that as a gap in this page, not a finding about Codex.
capabilities.establishedBy: The skills extraction behind the bundled-skills page; both skills directories on this machine. The Codex half is deliberately a non-claim.

capabilities.claudeCode: Definitions in .claude/agents/ or inline via --agents <json>. /subtask and /fork send work off and bring the result back; /workflows tracks multi-agent runs.
capabilities.codex: /agent and /subagents switch which agent thread you are typing at. SubagentStart and SubagentStop exist as hook points.
capabilities.establishedBy: Both command inventories; ~/.claude/agents/; the hook state keys in config.toml.

capabilities.claudeCode: A client. claude mcp manages servers; --mcp-config loads them from a file or string and --strict-mcp-config ignores everything else.
capabilities.codex: A client and a server: codex mcp-server starts Codex itself as an MCP server over stdio, so another agent can call it as a tool.
capabilities.establishedBy: codex --help; the flag tables on both index pages.

capabilities.claudeCode: claude -p plus flags: --output-format json|stream-json, --json-schema for structured output, --max-budget-usd, --input-format, --include-partial-messages.
capabilities.codex: codex exec with its own subcommands (resume, review), plus codex app-server — a protocol daemon that will emit its own JSON Schema and TypeScript bindings for you.
capabilities.establishedBy: Both flag tables and subcommand trees.

capabilities.claudeCode: Anthropic, with /setup-bedrock and /setup-vertex for the cloud resellers, --fallback-model when the default is overloaded, and --betas for API-key users.
capabilities.codex: OpenAI, with --oss and --local-provider lmstudio|ollama for running against a local model instead.

capabilities.claudeCode: None user-facing. Gating is internal: ten commands are in the binary but withheld from /help, and some skills register only when a check passes.
capabilities.codex: codex features list prints 100 switches with a maturity stage each, 40 of them on in this build, toggleable per-run with --enable/--disable or persisted with codex features enable.
capabilities.establishedBy: Both index pages; the feature table is codex features list verbatim.

capabilities.claudeCode: At the prompt. 129 of 143 entries are typed after a / — 96 native, 23 bundled skills, 10 hidden — leaving 14 shell subcommands.
capabilities.codex: In the shell. 68 of 122 entries are codex subcommands, against 54 typed after a / — the only one of the two where the shell side is the bigger half.
capabilities.establishedBy: Counted from the two inventories. Hidden commands are counted as slash commands on both sides, because that is how they are typed.

verdict.disclaimer: Opinion, not measurement. Everything else in this file was measured.
reachForClaudeCode: You want the session itself to be the workspace. Claude Code puts almost everything behind a /, including things Codex settles at launch — move to another directory, change effort, swap the model, background the whole session and get the terminal back.
You want to undo. /rewind has no counterpart on the Codex side of this page.
You lean on skills and subagents. 35 prompts ship in the binary, agents are files you write, and /subtask, /fork and /workflows exist to fan work out and collect it.
You want the model choice to include Bedrock or Vertex.
reachForCodex: You want the agent under a sandbox you can reason about — and reuse. Approval policy and sandbox policy are separate flags with named values, and codex sandbox will wrap any command, not just the agent's.
You are building on top of it. codex mcp-server makes Codex a tool other agents call; codex app-server hands you a protocol daemon with generated schema and TypeScript bindings.
You want the tool configured as data. One TOML file, layered profiles, and -c any.key=value for a single run.
You want to run against a local model — --oss with LM Studio or Ollama.
You want to see the feature flags rather than discover them.
verdict.andMostly: Neither list is a ranking, and the overlap is the real story: 43 jobs on this page have a command on both sides, several with the same name. Both ship hooks, MCP, plugins, skills, plan mode, a review command, a memory system and a desktop hand-off. Both also ship a command that imports the other one's setup, which tells you what the vendors expect you to be doing.
